tags.gist: Says CDRH asked the right questions, shares its access and least-burdensome aims, and offers refinements meant to make tests narrower, more auditable and cheaper.
Makes three proposals: grade risk by whether a function generates or presents a claim and who receives it; score claims against reference standards; bound open-endedness.
Proposes classifying by what an output asserts, not its wording: a function presents a claim originating elsewhere or generates one originating with the model.
Would assess risk on four dimensions: output significance, state of the condition, the user's ability to judge and act, and the design's characterizability.
Says no new evidence category is needed: score the clinical claims in open-ended output against a reference standard, emitted in structured form for higher-risk functions.
Sees open-endedness and variability as design decisions: bounding should be the primary expectation, and sponsors proposing competency evaluation must justify why bounding is impossible.
Says inferring competency works worst where consequences are greatest, and the testable analogue of a physician consulting or referring is deferral to human interpretation.
Draws the comparator from the local standard of care, never from the absence of interpretation, with absolute prespecified thresholds independent of being generative.
Treats monitoring as a complement, not a substitute: reduced premarket evidence shifts uncertainty onto patients, and the conditions for substitution rarely hold for high-risk functions.
Wants architectural safeguards required for high-risk functions, because their failing inputs cannot be enumerated and no control can target an undescribed failure.
Proposes three safeguards: validated quantified uncertainty at each stage, an independent secondary evaluation path, and structured deferral to humans when checks fail.
Would specify performance as finalized-case error rate by consequence, plus the deferral rate, scaling safeguards with risk profile whether supervised or autonomous.
Wants one risk framework for all AI functions, with substantial equivalence turning on characteristics: non-reproducible open-ended output should not be equivalent to a bounded predicate.
Wants generalizability measured with validated synthetic benchmarks, since real-world test sets leave each equipment, protocol and age combination too thin to measure.
Wants independent third parties to provide synthetic benchmarks, confidence resting on the conduct of an evaluation, and MDDT qualification expectations set for them.
Supports the risk-based approach and distinguishing among informational functions, and offers a refinement built on the paper's own qualifications and the IMDRF framework.
Finds the paper's own qualifications of its two-axis structure persuasive and aims to give them structural standing in the framework.
Endorses the paper's views that directiveness depends on substance, that disclaimers do not reduce it, and that non-evaluable measurement outputs may carry higher risk.
Endorses the paper's view that professionals are better placed than patients to spot wrong outputs, and that specialist-dependent functions are riskier for non-specialists.
Notes a cardiovascular risk score, the paper's non-directive example, prompts action when very high, so activity-axis position may depend on the output delivered.
Argues the analogous FDA and IMDRF matrices organize their axis around significance of the output, which is stable across phrasing, whereas directiveness reads as wording.
Sets out four dimensions: significance (present or generate claims), state of the condition, the user of the output, and characterizability (reproducible, bounded).
Makes traceability the organizing principle of the activity axis: presenting conveys claims from input or identified sources, generating originates them with the model.
Maps the distinction onto IMDRF's informing versus driving boundary: a function contributing its own clinical claim, even as an aid, is no longer informing.
Grades generating functions by claim kind: presenting is informational, then generating a measurement, a detection, a diagnosis or a management determination, in rising order.
Notes IMDRF groups detection, diagnosis and treatment together, and welcomes CDRH's view on whether the upper levels should be strictly ordered.
Separates what kind of claim a function generates from whether a qualified person evaluates it before effect, which belongs to the user dimension.
Clarifies: raw data is no claim; a function generates when it alters a claim's certainty, applies it beyond its source's scope, or synthesizes findings.
Applies the distinction per claim, not per device, consistent with the multiple-function approach, putting the evidentiary burden exactly on the judgment the model made.
Grounds the construct in natural language generation work on attribution to sources, faithfulness versus factuality, and intrinsic versus extrinsic content.
Warns a citation does not make an output presenting, citing hallucination rates in retrieval-grounded tools; claims must be demonstrably drawn from the source.
Says the distinction does not decide device status but tracks the decision-support exclusion: presenting functions for a reviewing professional may qualify, generating ones generally cannot.
Retains the consequence axis, graded critical, serious or non-serious as in IMDRF, and would express reversibility and time pressure on it.
Gives the user a structural place as a dimension assessed through three considerations, two about the user and one about the device.
Asks whether the user can judge the output; for subspecialty content only the specialist can, citing wrong AI suggestions sharply cutting inexperienced readers' accuracy.
Says design, not the user, sets whether an output's basis can be evaluated, which must be shown; explainability claimed to lower risk needs benchmarking.
Asks whether the user can act correctly within the established pathway: the same finding delivered outside that pathway, or to a patient, carries different risk.
Wants a dedicated user dimension rather than shifting patient-facing functions up the consequence axis, since the user changes error detection, not harm severity.
Shares the paper's recognition that patient- and generalist-facing functions bring real benefits; the dimension identifies what they must demonstrate, not discourages them.
Says the user dimension covers supervised versus autonomous operation and downstream safeguards, so no separate autonomy position on the activity axis is needed.
Proposes a fourth dimension of design properties, output determinism and bounding of input and output space, which set how much evidence is needed.
Defines the two properties: whether the design specifies reproducible output and by what mechanism, and whether inputs and outputs are constrained or open-ended.
Says a risk dimension must be known from design, not results; variability and openness raise the burden, which claim-level reproducibility then discharges.
Agrees that variation in safety-critical behavior such as diagnostic conclusions is a failure, while varied wording in a presented summary matters little.
Wants faithfulness, conveying the identified source accurately without addition, alteration or omission, required as a benchmarking element wherever a function presents claims.
Resolves conversational drift directly: a function that generates clinical content anywhere in an exchange takes that significance position for the whole exchange.
Says under- and over-escalation need not be incommensurable: for a defined condition they are sensitivity and specificity, prespecified and weighted by consequence.
Says the measurement and output-value issues arise for conventional software too, so the refinement should apply generally, though without a common risk profile.
Welcomes tailoring competency evaluation to intended use and risk, but questions its premise and limits of inference, offering an alternative making much of it unnecessary.
Observes that the competency approach rests on two attributed properties, open-ended inputs and outputs and output variability, quoting the paper's rationale.
Supports extending independence requirements to language-model adjudicators.
Notes the paper elsewhere frames open-endedness and variability conditionally, as properties devices may have, and calls that framing correct and important.
Says these properties are largely designed in; the framework should ask sponsors to show whether they hold, with bounded devices evaluated by established methods.
Says the licensing analogy needs careful examination, since these systems' licensing-style performance has not been shown to carry over to open clinical practice.
Cites a review finding licensing-style benchmarks near saturation while diagnostic and safety tasks score far lower, plus distraction and contamination effects.
Says inferring open-practice performance from structured assessment is not currently supported, so the framework should say what would make that inference reliable.
Argues models underweight rare must-not-miss diagnoses relative to trained clinicians, so competency inference is least reliable where consequence is greatest.
Says licensing presumes a physician who defers when unsure; deferral is directly testable, so validate it as a device property instead of inferring competency.
Shows bounding is routine for conventional AI and available for generative: prespecified prompts, curated retrieval, admissibility gates, claim sets, templates, constrained decoding.
Expects sponsors to bound functions where they can, earning a lighter evidentiary burden; functions left unbounded sit higher on the risk dimension with greater burden.
Lists bounding's limits, structure not correctness, degraded quality and an attack surface, so bounding mechanisms need their own verification and evidenced claims.
Recommends bounded inputs and outputs as the primary regulatory expectation, allowing competency-based evaluation only where a sponsor justifies that bounding is unachievable.
Where a rare condition cannot be adequately evidenced, exclude it from the authorized outputs and defer to humans rather than infer from adjacent competence.
Central recommendation: translate open-ended output into clinical claims that established kinds of valid scientific evidence can assess; no new evidence category needed.
Says a stated diagnosis is a claim scorable against a reference standard with conventional sensitivity and specificity, powered around traditional endpoints, for correctness and reproducibility.
Prefers higher-risk functions emit claims in structured form, scored directly without a judging model; any free-text claim extractor needs validation against human extraction.
Measures reproducibility per claim: the share of repeated runs, and of runs under irrelevant perturbation, where the function asserts the same claim.
Notes three limits: the extractor is a model, unanticipated claims escape scoring unless flagged against the authorized set, and a claim includes its certainty.
Says claim-level evaluation against independently adjudicated reference standards reduces reliance on sponsor benchmarks whose validity would need separate proof.
Says claim-level endpoints are conventional accuracy endpoints, so sample sizes and confidence intervals follow conventional methods per claim and consequence stratum.
Would have the four-dimension risk profile set the nature, rigor and amount of evidence: elements, test conditions, clinical confirmation and expected safeguards.
Maps characteristics to benchmarks: claim accuracy for generating, faithfulness for presenting, reproducibility for variable output, scope checks for open-ended, conversational elements for chat.
Says many Appendix A elements presuppose a conversational interface and would burden imaging measurement or segmentation functions without any safety return.
Wants detection addressed explicitly as a function type, since in imaging a missed finding produces a confident, complete-looking output with no error signal.
Where an existing regulation and guidance govern a function, such as quantitative imaging repeatability, a generative implementation should stay under them, not a parallel framework.
Agrees that no one comparator fits every device and the choice should follow intended use and deployment environment, as the paper's alternatives allow.
Makes the comparator the standard of care of the indicated environment: specialist with versus without the device, or a specialist panel for autonomous functions.
Rejects comparing with the care available in the device's absence, since absence changes benefit, not the consequence of errors; use the median specialist instead.
Would fix the median-specialist comparator from a documented representative sample and use it to set a prespecified absolute threshold, not a moving comparison.
Keeps care in the device's absence for the benefit-risk determination only; acceptance criteria should be absolute thresholds per condition, justified by error consequence.
Cites the first autonomous diagnostic authorization, which rested on prespecified absolute sensitivity and specificity thresholds against an independent reference standard.
Says generative and conventional devices for the same use and environment should face the same comparator and acceptance threshold.
Strongly recommends monitoring complement, not substitute for, premarket evidence: reduced evidence transfers discovery of uncertainty to patients while sponsors gain earlier entry.
Allows monitoring to compensate only where failures are detectable in monitored data, caught before harm, automatically mitigated, and output is reproducible.
Says those conditions rarely hold for functions generating diagnoses for serious conditions without prior qualified review, so the approach is inappropriate there.
Would build monitoring on premarket evidence made as complete as design permits, rejecting the premise that incomplete premarket characterization is inherent to these devices.
Supports the paper's monitoring approaches, matching each to a reason premarket evidence is incomplete: model evolution, output variability, input drift and open-endedness.
Agrees monitoring should vary with risk and would scale its intensity to whichever of the four reasons apply to a given device.
Warns zero decoding temperature does not guarantee reproducible output in production serving, so reproducibility should be demonstrated behaviorally, not asserted as a setting.
Notes conventional inference is deterministic only when configured so, while batch-composition dependence persists in generative serving regardless of settings.
Says fixed-weight bounded devices face mainly drift, while variable open-ended ones on third-party models face all four, so cadence and triggers should differ.
Stresses reproducibility still leaves monitoring necessary, since equipment and population shifts degrade unchanged devices; intensity should match the sources of variation present.
Would reduce proactive monitoring's scope and cadence where premarket evidence characterizes a conventional AI device across broad acquisition conditions and populations.
Supports machine-based supervisory monitoring, noting an EU-certified autonomous breast screening device already uses a supervisory layer that returns sites to full reading.
Wants a supervisory function treated as a device function in its own right, with specification, verification and validation, complementing premarket evidence rather than reducing it.
Recommends version pinning as a specification, contractual change notice, mandatory re-benchmarking on any model change, and a PCCP for anticipated changes.
Agrees a master file would not authorize the model and sponsors remain responsible; files may inform review but not substitute for device-level evidence.
Says the paper evaluates unreviewed functions' standalone performance but not how their risk can be controlled by design, and offers safeguards.
Says autonomy is no distinct class: a supervised stochastic open-ended function whose basis the supervisor cannot inspect carries comparable risk, so safeguards follow risk profile.
Offers three architectural properties that together make an unbounded failure space bounded and measurable, as controls for high-risk functions.
First safeguard: quantified uncertainty at each stage, validated against observed error and propagated forward, so unstable conclusions are withheld.
Second safeguard: an independent secondary path differing in task, data and architecture, catching confident single-model errors; disagreement blocks finalization.
Third safeguard: structured deferral to humans when validity checks fail, a finding falls outside the authorized set, paths disagree, or uncertainty exceeds threshold.
Scales safeguards with risk profile: conventional validation for lower, uncertainty with deferral for moderate, all three for higher including autonomous and patient-facing functions.
Would characterize performance as the error rate among finalized cases, with intervals and stratified by consequence, plus the deferral rate as an operating parameter.
Supports treating under- and over-deferral as failures, and wants both reported with a prespecified, justified operating point.
Illustrates that a supervised narrative CT reporting function generating unbounded claims still warrants full safeguards, since supervision removes none of its characteristics.
Contrasts two fracture detectors with identical use and user: stochastic open-ended versus reproducible bounded design yields a substantially different risk profile.
Wants CDRH to state explicitly that most of its recommendations are technology-agnostic, so the framework also reaches non-generative functions raising the same questions.
Notes the user's role and evaluation of unreviewed outputs are equally open for conventional AI devices and unaddressed by current guidance.
Says autonomy risk comes from absent human review, not model class, and wants autonomy handled as its own cross-cutting topic.
Says one framework with the fourth dimension can serve generative and conventional functions alike, consistent with FDA not regulating GenAI as such.
Explains why generative implementations need more scrutiny, reproducibility and bounding must be engineered, while stressing conventional AI's advantage is evaluability, not safety.
Keeps classification by intended use, with generative measurement, detection or diagnosis functions inside existing device types; no parallel classifications.
Wants substantial equivalence to turn on characteristics: a generative device with non-reproducible or open-ended output should not be equivalent to a bounded predicate.
Illustrates with a volumetric measurement, lesion detection and an added narrative function; existing substantial equivalence standards suffice, applied to new characteristics.
Strongly supports the generalizability element, synthetic data for small subgroups and third-party benchmarking, and says the three belong together.
Says generalizability deserves greater weight: as accuracy rises and benchmarks saturate, what matters is where remaining errors concentrate.
Shows a realistic real-world test set leaves each equipment, protocol and age combination too thin for confident estimates, and authorized devices rarely report subgroup data.
Supports real-world and ex-US data as the paper proposes, but says they enlarge a test set without filling thin strata and vary many factors together.
Lists synthetic data's strengths: coverage by design, one-factor variation, known reference standards, freedom from contamination, repeatability and boundary testing.
Finds synthetic data best suited to imaging, where input formation is modelable and outputs score against known references; less so for outcomes or clinician use.
Wants a synthetic benchmark to show realism by blinded expert discrimination, perceptible labeled findings, and agreement with real-world results for reference devices.
Would report synthetic and real-world results separately by default, combining them only under a prespecified method once agreement has been shown.
Answers the same-class concern with independence: a generator built on explicit anatomy and image-formation models, or an independent third-party benchmark, avoids shared blind spots.
Says synthetic data complements real-world evidence and does not replace it, extending evaluation to what real data cannot practically reach.
Where neither real nor synthetic data can evidence a condition, drop it from the authorized outputs and defer to human interpretation.
Sees third parties contributing most through synthetic benchmarks, bringing capability smaller sponsors lack, independence from the device, and comparability across devices.
Defines independence relative to the device under evaluation, noting device developers often build the best tools and MDDT already accepts their proposals.
Rests confidence on how an evaluation is run: prespecified with a hashed test set, automatically scored, reported identically to FDA and sponsor, and fully auditable.
Keeps acceptance decisions with FDA and sponsors; FDA should qualify tools, not designate providers, with non-discriminatory access and alternative evidence allowed.
Recommends retaining generalizability as a distinct evidence element for all AI devices, with performance reported across intended-use strata, not only in aggregate.
Recommends recognizing validated synthetic benchmarks as evidence of generalizability in submissions, PCCP verification and postmarket re-benchmarking.
Recommends publishing MDDT qualification expectations for synthetic benchmarking tools, prioritizing proposals that address the paper's evidence gaps.
Recommends FDA keep supporting independent benchmarking capability through existing research and qualification mechanisms.
Recommends postmarket expectations allow reduced proactive monitoring where broad premarket generalizability evidence exists for a conventional AI device.
Appreciates early stakeholder engagement, noting several of its recommendations would raise evidentiary expectations for the commenter's own device class.
Says the field's main risk is an early avoidable failure in a high-consequence setting, not over-demanding regulation; precision and proportion serve all.
Illustrates the distinction with impression drafting: restating documented findings presents, while adding an untraceable suspicion or follow-up interval generates.
Illustrates with serial oncology reports: summarizing presents, concluding treatment failed generates, applying named response criteria presents, measuring images generates.
Illustrates with a cholesterol value: guideline lookup presents, while textually identical model output citing the guideline generates, so citations prove nothing.
Illustrates with consensus diagnostic criteria: applying them to documented findings presents, a model producing the same sentence generates; omitting conditions breaks faithfulness.
Illustrates with a wearable: classifications, alerts and risk scores are generated claims, as are measurements computed from raw sensor signals.
Illustrates with renal dosing: returning the labeled adjustment presents and needs faithfulness evidence; deriving a dose from the clinical picture generates a management claim.
Profiles a medication-history summary for a pharmacist as presenting, source-linked and verifiable: lower risk, faithfulness benchmarking including omissions.
Profiles a wearable atrial fibrillation notification as a generated detection for a serious condition to a lay user: moderate risk, uncertainty with deferral.
Profiles an intensive-care deterioration score as a generated detection for a critical condition: moderate to higher, showing why significance, not directiveness, should grade it.
Profiles a consumer skin-lesion app as a generated diagnosis to a lay user: higher risk under either implementation, with all three safeguards.
Profiles a patient-facing emergency-care advisor as a generated management determination: higher risk, all safeguards, escalation scored as sensitivity and specificity.
Illustrates bounding by intended use, such as closed finding vocabularies for report drafting and closed dispositions with mandatory escalation for conversational triage.
Illustrates structure-first versus text-first knee MRI reporting: structured findings are scored directly, free text needs a validated extractor.
Illustrates claim-level reproducibility: twenty runs plus perturbation per case, agreement recorded per finding and stratified by consequence.
